title: King Agrippa (I)
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: Hyman reports that he was the son of Aristobulus son of Herod, whom Mariamne, granddaughter of Hyrcanus son of King Yannai, bore to him, as explained at length in Yosippon, in the Jewish War, chapter 17. Hyman describes him as an upright king who reigned six years, did much good for Israel, and began to build a lofty wall around Jerusalem. This Agrippa is mentioned in Pesachim 117b: he was accustomed to eat at the ninth hour. The Rashbam explains that he was one of the Hasmonean kings, and Tosafot there, s.v. Afilu, disagree with him, for in Mishnah Sotah 41a they said: when he reached “from among your brothers you shall set a king over you,” his eyes streamed with tears; they said to him, “Do not fear; you are our brother.” Rashi explains: he was a king of Israel of the seed of Herod. Hyman supports the Rashbam, since on his mother’s side he was of the Hasmonean seed, and on his father’s side of Herod’s seed.

He is likewise mentioned in Mishnah Bikkurim 3:4, where they said: “Even King Agrippa takes the basket on his shoulder.” Pesachim 64b relates that once he wished to know the number of Israel and commanded the High Priest to count the Passover offerings. In Ketubot 17a they said of him that he would step aside before a bride, and the sages praised him.

Vayikra Rabbah 3:5 relates that once Agrippas wished to offer a thousand burnt-offerings and commanded the High Priest not to offer for anyone else that day besides him. A poor man came with two turtledoves and offered them, and the king told him that he had done well. In Avodah Zarah 55a: “Agrippas, the general [Dikdukei Soferim: Agrippa the general] of Agrippus, asked Rabban Gamliel [the Elder],” and Rashi explains that he was a gentile appointed over the soldiers in the days of King Agrippa.

Hyman reports that Yosippon explicitly states that he left after him three daughters and one young son, also named Agrippa; since he was still young, he did not reign in his place, and the land of Judea was annexed to the Roman province under a governor and procurator.

Afterward, before the destruction, his son Agrippa reigned, but he had only the shadow of a king. Hyman suggests that this Agrippa is the one mentioned in Sukkah 27a: “The steward of King Agrippa asked Rabbi Eliezer,” and it is known that Rabbi Eliezer lived before the destruction.

notes.text: Supplied Pesachimקיז: is117b, retained alongside returned Davidson107b’s ninth-hour meal. Bikkurim3:4 uses the supplied halakhah number. Hyman’s six-year reign, genealogy, Rashbam defense and tentative identification of the younger Agrippa are attributed; no fresh historical or authority merge.

The consulted Pesachim 107b names Agrippa eating at the ninth hour; supplied 117b remains alongside it. The six-year reign, genealogy and defense of Rashbam remain Hyman’s reported historical argument, not independent verification of the exact Yosippon or commentary editions. The younger Agrippa identification remains tentative, and the general of Agrippa is not merged with the king.
